claim: Interval timing is a fundamental component of action and is susceptible to motor-related temporal distortions.
source: Interval timing is a fundamental component of action and is susceptible to motor-related temporal distortions.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that frames the research context, drawing on established scientific understanding.

claim: Previous studies have shown that concurrent movement biases temporal estimates.
source: Previous studies have shown that concurrent movement biases temporal estimates, but have primarily considered self-modulated movement only.
evidence: This claim references prior research findings without specific citations in this sentence, but is supported by citations elsewhere in the manuscript.

claim: Higher viscosity led to shorter perceived durations.
source: Results demonstrated that higher viscosity led to shorter perceived durations.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experiments reported in the manuscript, supported by experimental data.

claim: The biasing effects of viscosity arose from perceptual mechanisms, instead of biases in decision making.
source: Using a drift-diffusion model and a Bayesian observer model, we confirmed these biasing effects arose from perceptual mechanisms, instead of biases in decision making.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling analyses (drift-diffusion model and Bayesian observer model) applied to the experimental data.

claim: Environmental perturbations are an important factor in movement-related temporal distortions.
source: These findings suggest that environmental perturbations are an important factor in movement-related temporal distortions, and enhance the current understanding of the interactions of motor activity and cognitive processes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and their interpretation.

claim: Central pattern generators produce basic locomotion in many organisms and yield balanced, rhythmic motor output via the oscillatory properties of inhibitory interneurons.
source: For example, central pattern generators produce basic locomotion in many organisms and yield balanced, rhythmic motor output via the oscillatory properties of inhibitory interneurons (Guertin, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Guertin, 2009.

claim: Many behaviors rely on the explicit awareness of time.
source: At greater levels of complexity, many behaviors rely on the explicit awareness of time (Buhusi and Meck, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Buhusi and Meck, 2005.

claim: Subjective time is not always veridical and is subject to distortion across many organisms.
source: Subjective time is not always veridical, however; in fact, across many organisms, it is subject to distortion (Malapani and Fairhurst, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Malapani and Fairhurst, 2002.

claim: Temporal distortions can arise from changes in perception, attention, and memory processes.
source: As described by Matthews and Meck, 2016, temporal distortions can arise from changes in perception, attention, and memory processes, and are proposed to be directly related to the vividness and ease of representation of a timed event.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Matthews and Meck, 2016.

claim: Subjective time on the scale of milliseconds to seconds is influenced by movement duration.
source: For example, it has been shown that subjective time on the scale of milliseconds to seconds is influenced by movement duration (Yon et al., 2017), speed (Yokosaka et al., 2015), and direction (Tomassini and Morrone, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yon et al., 2017.

claim: Subjective time on the scale of milliseconds to seconds is influenced by movement speed.
source: For example, it has been shown that subjective time on the scale of milliseconds to seconds is influenced by movement duration (Yon et al., 2017), speed (Yokosaka et al., 2015), and direction (Tomassini and Morrone, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yokosaka et al., 2015.

claim: Subjective time on the scale of milliseconds to seconds is influenced by movement direction.
source: For example, it has been shown that subjective time on the scale of milliseconds to seconds is influenced by movement duration (Yon et al., 2017), speed (Yokosaka et al., 2015), and direction (Tomassini and Morrone, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tomassini and Morrone, 2016.

claim: Timed events accompanied by arm movements that are short undergo compression.
source: More specifically, timed events accompanied by arm movements that are short (Yon et al., 2017), rapid (Yokosaka et al., 2015), or directed toward the body (Tomassini and Morrone, 2016) undergo compression.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yon et al., 2017.

claim: Timed events accompanied by arm movements that are rapid undergo compression.
source: More specifically, timed events accompanied by arm movements that are short (Yon et al., 2017), rapid (Yokosaka et al., 2015), or directed toward the body (Tomassini and Morrone, 2016) undergo compression.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yokosaka et al., 2015.

claim: Timed events accompanied by arm movements directed toward the body undergo compression.
source: More specifically, timed events accompanied by arm movements that are short (Yon et al., 2017), rapid (Yokosaka et al., 2015), or directed toward the body (Tomassini and Morrone, 2016) undergo compression.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tomassini and Morrone, 2016.

claim: Organisms use feedback information to update current and future movement plans when perturbations are encountered.
source: When these perturbations are encountered, organisms use feedback information to update current and future movement plans (Shadmehr et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shadmehr et al., 2010.

claim: Participants were required to time auditory tone intervals while moving a robotic arm manipulandum through environments with varying degrees of viscosity.
source: Participants were required to time auditory tone intervals while moving a robotic arm manipulandum through environments with varying degrees of viscosity.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure used in the study.

claim: Viscosity successfully decreased movement distance in the temporal categorization task.
source: In the categorization experiment, we demonstrate that viscosity successfully decreased movement distance, and that this decrease was associated with underestimation of time intervals.
evidence: This is a finding from Experiment 1, supported by experimental data.

claim: The decrease in movement distance was associated with underestimation of time intervals.
source: In the categorization experiment, we demonstrate that viscosity successfully decreased movement distance, and that this decrease was associated with underestimation of time intervals.
evidence: This is a finding from Experiment 1, supported by experimental data.

claim: The modulation of time perception by viscosity was a result of interval timing and not a decision-related bias.
source: We verified that this modulation was a result of interval timing and not a decision-related bias by applying a recently developed drift-diffusion model of timing (Balcı and Simen, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling analysis using a drift-diffusion model, with citation to Balcı and Simen, 2014.

claim: In the reproduction experiment, all participants tended to overestimate durations.
source: In the reproduction experiment, all participants tended to overestimate durations, but viscosity was related to decreased overestimation and greater central tendency.
evidence: This is a finding from Experiment 2, supported by experimental data.

claim: Viscosity was related to decreased overestimation and greater central tendency in the reproduction experiment.
source: In the reproduction experiment, all participants tended to overestimate durations, but viscosity was related to decreased overestimation and greater central tendency.
evidence: This is a finding from Experiment 2, supported by experimental data.

claim: The effect of viscosity on time perception in the reproduction experiment was a result of perceptual bias rather than increased noise in the measurement and production processes.
source: We utilized a Bayesian Observer Model (Jazayeri and Shadlen, 2010; Remington et al., 2018) to verify that this effect was a result of perceptual bias rather than increased noise in the measurement and production processes.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling analysis using a Bayesian Observer Model, with citations to Jazayeri and Shadlen, 2010 and Remington et al., 2018.

claim: Movement distance has a direct influence on perceived interval length, regardless of whether this parameter is modulated by volitional or environmental factors.
source: Overall, these results suggest that movement distance has a direct influence on perceived interval length, regardless of whether this parameter is modulated by volitional or environmental factors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined results of both experiments.

claim: Allowance of movement enhanced temporal perception by reducing variability in a previous study.
source: Allowance of movement enhanced temporal perception by reducing variability (i.e. lower coefficient of variation).
evidence: This refers to findings from a previous study by the authors (Wiener et al., 2019).

claim: No impact of viscosity was observed on relative hand position.
source: However, no impact of viscosity was observed on relative hand position [F(3,81)=1.595, p=0.197], suggesting that movement had little impact on the ability of subjects to employ this strategy.
evidence: This is a finding from Experiment 1, supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: No effect of viscosity was observed on the coefficient of variation in Experiment 1.
source: No effect of viscosity was observed on the CV [F(3,81)=0.377, p=0.77; BF10=0.073] (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from Experiment 1, supported by experimental data, statistical analysis, and Bayes Factor.

claim: Large inter-individual differences in the average distances moved by different subjects were observed.
source: However, we observed large inter-individual differences in the average distances moved by different subjects.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis of Experiment 1.

claim: Subjects were largely consistent in their movement distances across viscosity conditions.
source: That is, some subjects moved a lot, whereas some moved very little; notably, subjects were largely consistent in their movement distances across viscosity conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis of Experiment 1, with reference to a figure.

claim: Subjects who moved more also exerted more force.
source: Similarly, subjects who moved more also exerted more force in doing so; we further observed that the effect of viscosity on movement distance and force were correlated between subjects [Pearson r = −0.73, p<0.001; Spearman r = −0.88, p<0.001].
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis of Experiment 1, supported by correlation statistics.

claim: Only a weak correlation was found between the effect of viscosity on movement distance and the bisection point.
source: Here, we found only a weak correlation between the effect of viscosity on movement distance and the bisection point [Pearson r = −0.286, p=0.1395; Spearman r = −0.35, p=0.067].
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis of Experiment 1, supported by correlation statistics.

claim: The correlation between the effect of viscosity on force and bisection point was very weak.
source: Similarly, the correlation between the effect of viscosity on force was also very weak [Pearson r = 0.147, p=0.45; Spearman r = 0.221, p=0.25], suggesting that the effect of viscosity did not covary with individual differences in movement distance or force.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis of Experiment 1, supported by correlation statistics.

claim: Precision improved with greater movement, but only when no impediments from a viscous movement environment existed.
source: This indicates that precision again improved with greater movement, but only when no impediments from a viscous movement environment existed.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings from the within-subject median split analysis of Experiment 1.

claim: A shift in the drift rate towards one of the decision boundaries is interpreted as evidence in favor of a shift in the perceptual evidence.
source: A shift in the drift rate towards one of these boundaries is interpreted as evidence in favor of a shift in the perceptual evidence, whereas a change in the threshold boundary could be interpreted as a change in the decision layer (Voss et al., 2004; Hagura et al., 2017; Bogacz et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of drift diffusion model parameters, supported by citations.

claim: A change in the threshold boundary could be interpreted as a change in the decision layer.
source: A shift in the drift rate towards one of these boundaries is interpreted as evidence in favor of a shift in the perceptual evidence, whereas a change in the threshold boundary could be interpreted as a change in the decision layer (Voss et al., 2004; Hagura et al., 2017; Bogacz et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of drift diffusion model parameters, supported by citations.

claim: The Duration Model which included all four DDM parameters varying with duration was best able to account for subject data.
source: For the Duration Model, we initially observed that a model which included all four DDM parameters varying with duration (v,a,t,z) was best able to account for subject data [Full model DIC = 6967.01; v,a,t model DIC = 7350.09; v,a model DIC = 8076.33; v model DIC = 9514.65; empty model DIC = 15677.96].
evidence: This is a finding from the drift diffusion modeling analysis, supported by model comparison statistics (DIC values).

claim: The Duration Model was able to produce a similar pattern to subject data for both choice and RT.
source: Posterior predictive checks of the data additionally demonstrated that the Duration Model was able to produce a similar pattern to subject data for both choice and RT (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from the drift diffusion modeling analysis, supported by posterior predictive checks and figure reference.

claim: The only significant correlation observed between DDM parameters and the shift in BP was for the drift rate.
source: Here, the only significant correlation observed was for the drift rate [Pearson r = −0.5132, p=0.0052; Spearman r = −0.7865, p<0.001], and not for any other parameter (all p>0.05).
evidence: This is a finding from the drift diffusion modeling analysis, supported by correlation statistics.

claim: The correlation between drift rate and BP shift was significantly greater than for all other parameters.
source: A Fisher's Z-test comparing this correlation confirmed that it was significantly greater than for all other parameters (see Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the drift diffusion modeling analysis, supported by statistical comparison (Fisher's Z-test) and table reference.

claim: No impact on the variance of reproduced estimates was observed, with the CV remaining stable across all viscosities in Experiment 2.
source: No impact on the variance of reproduced estimates was observed, with the CV remaining stable across all viscosities [F(3,51)=0.691, p = 0.562; BF10=0.016] (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from Experiment 2, supported by experimental data, statistical analysis, Bayes Factor, and figure reference.

claim: No correlation was found between the effects of viscosity on Movement Distance and Force in Experiment 2.
source: Unlike Experiment 1, we found no correlation between the effects of viscosity on Movement Distance and Force [Pearson r = −0.16, p=0.52; Spearman r = −0.14, p=0.55], suggesting the correlation observed in Experiment 1 was primarily driven by some subjects moving very little.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis of Experiment 2, supported by correlation statistics.

claim: No between-subject correlation was observed between the effects of viscosity on movement distance and duration reproduction in Experiment 2.
source: Additionally, we observed no between-subject correlation between the effects of viscosity on movement distance and duration reproduction [Pearson r = 0.07, p=0.75; Spearman r = 0.19, p=0.44], nor on force and duration reproduction [Pearson r = 0.008, p=0.97; Spearman r = −0.23, p=0.34] (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis of Experiment 2, supported by correlation statistics and figure reference.

claim: No between-subject correlation was observed between the effects of viscosity on force and duration reproduction in Experiment 2.
source: Additionally, we observed no between-subject correlation between the effects of viscosity on movement distance and duration reproduction [Pearson r = 0.07, p=0.75; Spearman r = 0.19, p=0.44], nor on force and duration reproduction [Pearson r = 0.008, p=0.97; Spearman r = −0.23, p=0.34] (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis of Experiment 2, supported by correlation statistics and figure reference.

claim: Production noise was found to decrease with higher viscosities in a non-linear manner.
source: More specifically, production noise was found to decrease with higher viscosities; however, this effect was not linear, with the only difference being for zero viscosity estimates higher than all others.
evidence: This is a finding from the Bayesian Observer Model analysis.

claim: No effect of viscosity was observed on the measurement noise parameter in the Bayesian Observer Model.
source: No effect of viscosity was observed on the measurement noise parameter (m) [F(3,51)=1.212, p = 0.315].
evidence: This is a finding from the Bayesian Observer Model analysis, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Only the offset term significantly correlated with the underestimation effect in the Bayesian Observer Model.
source: As with the DDM results of Experiment 1, we further explored whether the linear nature of the shift in b could best explain the observed underestimation of duration by calculating the slope of a regression line for each parameter against viscosity and compared that to the change in reproduced duration. Only the offset term significantly correlated with the underestimation effect [Pearson = 0.7332, p < 0.001; Spearman = 0.709, p<0.001].
evidence: This is a finding from the Bayesian Observer Model analysis, supported by correlation statistics.

claim: The effect of viscosity was not significant in the Production Model.
source: We further note that, for the Production Model, the effect of viscosity was not significant [F(3,51)=0.871, p=0.462], suggesting that the model was not simply shifted from the true response.
evidence: This is a finding from the Bayesian Observer Model comparison, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Systematically impeding movement during interval timing leads to a subsequent compression of perceived duration.
source: The above experiments demonstrate that systematically impeding movement during interval timing leads to a subsequent compression of perceived duration.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the results of both experiments.

claim: Time perception is highly sensitive to movement.
source: These findings complement previous work showing that time perception is highly sensitive to movement (Yon et al., 2017; Yokosaka et al., 2015; Tomassini and Morrone, 2016), and here we confirm a case in which movement parameters (e.g., length and duration) did not have to be self-modulated to induce these distortions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and the current study's findings.

claim: Movement parameters did not have to be self-modulated to induce temporal distortions.
source: These findings complement previous work showing that time perception is highly sensitive to movement (Yon et al., 2017; Yokosaka et al., 2015; Tomassini and Morrone, 2016), and here we confirm a case in which movement parameters (e.g., length and duration) did not have to be self-modulated to induce these distortions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current study's findings.

claim: Increased viscosity shifted the BP such that subjects responded 'long' less often in the temporal categorization task.
source: In the temporal categorization task, we found that increased viscosity, on average, shifted the BP such that subjects responded 'long' less often.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Experiment 1.

claim: The drift rate parameter linearly shifted from the 'long' to the 'short' boundary with increasing viscosity.
source: The only significant contributor was the drift rate parameter, which linearly shifted from the 'long' to the 'short' boundary with increasing viscosity.
evidence: This is a finding from the drift diffusion modeling analysis of Experiment 1.

claim: Participants exhibited an overestimation bias when reproducing the interval duration in Experiment 2.
source: Participants exhibited an overestimation bias when reproducing the interval duration, a result previously shown in motor reproduction of auditory intervals (Shi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding from Experiment 2, supported by experimental data and citation to previous work.

claim: The degree of overestimation decreased as a function of viscosity in Experiment 2.
source: However, the degree of overestimation decreased as a function of viscosity, confirming the compression effect seen in the temporal categorization task.
evidence: This is a finding from Experiment 2.

claim: A linear shift in perceptual bias as a function of viscosity was observed using the Bayesian observer model.
source: Using a Bayesian observer model (Jazayeri and Shadlen, 2010; Remington et al., 2018), we observed a linear shift in perceptual bias as a function of viscosity, further supporting a purely perceptual effect of movement slowing on timing.
evidence: This is a finding from the Bayesian Observer Model analysis, supported by citations.

claim: Viscosity manipulation leads to interval underestimation.
source: The results between experiments converge on the finding that viscosity manipulation leads to interval underestimation (reflected in the bias parameters).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the results of both experiments.

claim: Timing precision was generally unaffected by viscosity manipulations.
source: Further, timing precision was generally unaffected by our manipulations.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the results of both experiments.

claim: The CV remained constant across viscosities in the temporal categorization task.
source: In the temporal categorization task, the CV remained constant across viscosities; the only notable CV effect was revealed by the median split analysis, in which trials with greater movement led to greater precision for the zero viscosity condition.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Experiment 1.

claim: Trials with greater movement led to greater precision for the zero viscosity condition in the temporal categorization task.
source: In the temporal categorization task, the CV remained constant across viscosities; the only notable CV effect was revealed by the median split analysis, in which trials with greater movement led to greater precision for the zero viscosity condition.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Experiment 1.

claim: Free movement can improve timing precision only in unrestricted movement environments.
source: This was in agreement with our previous study demonstrating a movement-related enhancement in temporal precision estimates (Wiener et al., 2019), and suggests that free movement can improve timing precision only in unrestricted movement environments.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of Experiment 1 and comparison to previous work.

claim: Viscosity did not affect the variability of estimation (CV) in the temporal reproduction task.
source: The temporal reproduction task also showed that viscosity did not affect the variability of estimation (CV), but interestingly, may have been associated with greater uncertainty as indicated by increased central tendency of reproduction slopes.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Experiment 2.

claim: Viscosity may have been associated with greater uncertainty as indicated by increased central tendency of reproduction slopes.
source: The temporal reproduction task also showed that viscosity did not affect the variability of estimation (CV), but interestingly, may have been associated with greater uncertainty as indicated by increased central tendency of reproduction slopes.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Experiment 2, with some speculation.

claim: Movement in the temporal categorization task had utilitarian value as participants could strategically approach candidate targets.
source: As mentioned above, in our first experiment we allowed movement, while in the second experiment we required it. Additionally, movement in the temporal categorization task had utilitarian value; participants could strategically approach candidate targets, and thus movement offered the potential to improve performance by shortening RTs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the task design and its implications.

claim: Movement in the temporal reproduction task did not provide a decision-making advantage.
source: Movement in the temporal reproduction task did not provide this decision-making advantage, but notably the perceptual biases due to viscosity maintained the same directionality across experiments.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the task design and its implications.

claim: The perceptual biases due to viscosity maintained the same directionality across experiments.
source: Movement in the temporal reproduction task did not provide this decision-making advantage, but notably the perceptual biases due to viscosity maintained the same directionality across experiments.
evidence: This is a comparison of findings across both experiments.

claim: Movement influenced similar temporal estimation mechanisms despite methodological differences between experiments.
source: That is, in response to viscosity, the BP parameter in Experiment one and the perceptual bias parameter in Experiment 2 shifted upwards and downwards respectively, in accordance with temporal compression. This suggests that movement influenced similar temporal estimation mechanisms, and despite methodological differences, the biasing effect of viscous environments was robust under different task demands.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing findings across both experiments.

claim: The biasing effect of viscous environments was robust under different task demands.
source: That is, in response to viscosity, the BP parameter in Experiment one and the perceptual bias parameter in Experiment 2 shifted upwards and downwards respectively, in accordance with temporal compression. This suggests that movement influenced similar temporal estimation mechanisms, and despite methodological differences, the biasing effect of viscous environments was robust under different task demands.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing findings across both experiments.

claim: Subjects were not required to time their movements but were rather using their movements for timing.
source: One additional note regarding this work is that subjects were not required to time their movements but were rather using their movements for timing.
evidence: This is a clarification about the nature of the task.

claim: The ancillary movement patterns influenced the perceived timing.
source: We believe the distinction here is important, as the ancillary movement patterns nevertheless influenced the perceived timing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The duration of tactile stimulus was perceived as longer when the avatar was congruent to concurrent movement.
source: (Press et al., 2014) presented tactile stimulation to participants' fingers during movement or while stationary as they viewed congruent or incongruent hand avatars displayed on a screen. The duration of the tactile stimulus was perceived as longer when the avatar was congruent to concurrent movement.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Press et al., 2014.

claim: Judgments of auditory stimulus duration were biased towards the duration of the movement in the Yon et al. 2017 study.
source: (Yon et al., 2017) similarly found that when participants executed finger movements of a pre-specified duration and listened to an auditory stimulus with an independently selected duration, judgments were biased towards the duration of the movement.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yon et al., 2017.

claim: Durations presented during 'far' reaches were perceived as longer in the Yon et al. 2017 study.
source: They followed this with a separate experiment focused on manipulating movement distance as a proxy for movement duration (with the knowledge that farther reaches typically take longer); participants reached towards targets along a flat workspace with variable distances while a concurrent auditory duration was presented. Durations presented during 'far' reaches were again perceived as longer.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yon et al., 2017.

claim: In the current experiments, movements were scaled exclusively in the spatial, but not temporal domain as a function of viscosity.
source: This bears similarity to our experiments here, with a few key distinctions: in our experiments, movements were scaled exclusively in the spatial, but not temporal domain as a function of viscosity (i.e. movement distance, but not movement duration, scaled with viscosity).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design and findings.

claim: The Yon experiments relied on volitional modulation for task success.
source: Additionally, the Yon experiments relied on volitional modulation for task success (e.g. being trained to make 'short' and 'long' movements or reach 'near' and 'far').
evidence: This is a description of the Yon et al. 2017 experimental design.

claim: The viscosity manipulation affected movement distance without any change in task demands.
source: Our manipulation affected movement distance without any change in task demands; that is, the manipulated sensory feedback (via the somatosensory system) offered no explicit benefit or detriment to completing the task.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Even though participants knew that demands did not change with viscosity, the manipulation still induced temporal biases.
source: We believe this is a critical insight given by our study; even though participants knew that demands did not change with viscosity, the manipulation still induced temporal biases – presumably without conscious awareness.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Complementary mechanisms of temporal biasing by movement distance and duration exist that are often conflated due to distance-duration correlations.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest complementary mechanisms of temporal biasing by movement distance and duration that are often conflated due to distance-duration correlations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the current findings with previous work.

claim: Visual intervals demarcated by pairs of visual flashes were compressed during fast hand movement in the Yokosaka et al. 2015 study.
source: For example, Yokosaka et al., 2015 found that visual intervals demarcated by pairs of visual flashes were compressed during fast hand movement, whereas in our experiment we show that slowing down movement leads to compression.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yokosaka et al., 2015.

claim: Tactile intervals were compressed during hand movement in the Tomassini et al. 2014 study.
source: Additionally, Tomassini and colleagues (Tomassini et al., 2014) reported that tactile intervals were compressed during hand movement.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tomassini et al., 2014.

claim: Many of the distortive effects of movement can be linked to whether an interval is filled or unfilled.
source: Considering these examples, a crucial note–as highlighted in Iwasaki et al., 2017–is that many of the distortive effects of movement can be linked to whether an interval is filled or unfilled.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Iwasaki et al., 2017.

claim: Biological motion is timed more precisely than constant motion for sub- and supra-second intervals.
source: When timing the duration of a dot moving across a screen with different movement profiles, biological motion (compared to constant motion) is timed more precisely for sub- and supra-second intervals, and more accurately for sub-second intervals (Gavazzi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gavazzi et al., 2013.

claim: The perceived duration of a human light-point display was expanded compared to a static or non-biological motion display.
source: Wang and Jiang, 2012 found that the perceived duration of a human light-point display was expanded compared to a static or non-biological motion display, and this effect persisted when the dot positions were scrambled but retained local kinematics.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang and Jiang, 2012.

claim: Hand tracking overall improved accuracy and precision in timing a dot stimulus, irrespective of the movement type.
source: Carlini and French, 2014 asked participants to time a dot stimulus moving across a screen that they either tracked with their finger, or viewed passively. Hand tracking overall improved accuracy and precision, but the improvement occurred irrespective of the movement type (biological motion, constant velocity, or sharp 'triangular' velocity profile).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Carlini and French, 2014.

claim: Biological motion was timed most accurately and precisely with or without manual tracking.
source: Additionally, biological motion was timed most accurately and precisely with or without manual tracking.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Carlini and French, 2014.

claim: Concurrent movement can increase the accuracy of non-biological motion timing to biological motion levels.
source: This highlights a benefit of concurrent movement that can increase the accuracy of non-biological motion timing to biological motion levels.
evidence: This is an interpretation of findings from Carlini and French, 2014.

claim: The compressing effect of viscosity would occur more strongly for non-biological motion because it is more susceptible to motor influences.
source: For example, would the compressing effect of viscosity occur more strongly for non-biological motion because it is more susceptible to motor influences? If we were to administer a similar manual tracking task, we predict that this would be the case.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction about future experiments.

claim: This work highlights the importance of sensory feedback in timing.
source: This novel contribution to the existing body of research highlights the importance of sensory feedback in timing, whereas the study of movement-induced time distortions has focused primarily on feedforward effects.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and their context in the literature.

claim: Interval timing in the brain utilizes multiple streams of sensory information and distributed timing circuits to form a unified percept of duration.
source: These complementary accounts enrich the current understanding of the coupling of movement and time perception, and support the longstanding notion that interval timing in the brain utilizes multiple streams of sensory information and distributed timing circuits to form a unified percept of duration (Chen and Vroomen, 2013; Bausenhart et al., 2014; Wiener et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen and Vroomen, 2013; Bausenhart et al., 2014; Wiener et al., 2011.

claim: Previous research has shown motor system involvement in time perception, even when no timed motor response is required.
source: As described above, previous research has shown motor system involvement in time perception, even when no timed motor response is required (Nani et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nani et al., 2019.

claim: Temporal categorization has been linked to motor system processing and neural populations within the supplementary motor area (SMA).
source: Further, temporal categorization, as employed here has been linked to motor system processing and neural populations within the supplementary motor area (SMA), a region highly implicated in timing (Schwartze et al., 2012; Mendoza et al., 2018; Méndez et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schwartze et al., 2012; Mendoza et al., 2018; Méndez et al., 2014.

claim: The results align with A Theory of Magnitude (ATOM), which outlines common neural circuitry between spatial, temporal, and numerosity representations in the brain.
source: Most saliently, our results align with A Theory of Magnitude (ATOM), an account outlining common neural circuitry between spatial, temporal, and numerosity representations in the brain (Walsh, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Walsh, 2003.

claim: The manipulation scaled spatial characteristics of movement, and subsequently led to a scaling down of perceived duration.
source: The manipulation we introduced scaled spatial characteristics of movement, and subsequently led to a scaling down of perceived duration.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Viscosity was introduced via sensorimotor channels but had a cross-modal effect on auditory timing.
source: A relevant consideration here is that viscosity was introduced via sensorimotor channels but had a cross-modal effect on auditory timing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The two channels of temporal processing (motor and auditory) were not redundant.
source: Our results suggest that the two channels of temporal processing were not redundant; if this had been the case, there would have been no effect of movement on the separate auditory estimate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Noisy auditory estimates reaped a benefit from integrating motor information with higher precision, at the cost of a slight bias.
source: Combined with the knowledge that movement can also bias timing, we suggest that noisy auditory estimates in our experiments reaped a benefit from integrating motor information with higher precision, at the cost of a slight bias.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings, drawing on optimal cue combination principles.

claim: Motor control is an extension of ongoing cognitive computations.
source: Notable work in recent years has strongly suggested that motor control is an extension of ongoing cognitive computations (Lepora and Pezzulo, 2015; Resulaj et al., 2009), and adopting an integrated view of cognition-action pathways is a promising avenue for understanding these disorders and developing therapies that exploit these links.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lepora and Pezzulo, 2015; Resulaj et al., 2009.

claim: Core timing networks in the brain overlap substantially with the motor circuitry targeted by neural degeneration in Parkinson's and Huntington's Diseases.
source: For example, in the case of Parkinson's (PD) and Huntington's Diseases (HD), core timing networks in the brain overlap substantially with the motor circuitry targeted by neural degeneration, such as the basal ganglia (Obeso et al., 2000; Obeso et al., 2014; Browne et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Obeso et al., 2000; Obeso et al., 2014; Browne et al., 1997.

claim: Motor deficits in Parkinson's and Huntington's Diseases are often accompanied by timing deficits and other cognitive abnormalities.
source: Motor deficits in these diseases are often accompanied by timing deficits (Avanzino et al., 2016) and other cognitive abnormalities (Robbins and Cools, 2014; Paulsen, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Avanzino et al., 2016; Robbins and Cools, 2014; Paulsen, 2011.

claim: Some studies have shown that hyperactivity associated with ADHD can boost cognitive control performance.
source: The excessive motoric activity (i.e. hyperactivity) associated with the disorder is typically seen as disruptive, but interestingly, some studies have shown that it can boost cognitive control performance (Rapport et al., 2009; Hartanto et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rapport et al., 2009; Hartanto et al., 2016.

claim: Timing deficits are present in ADHD.
source: In light of the timing deficits present in ADHD (Plummer and Humphrey, 2009), it would be interesting to explore the extent movement can provide a similar benefit to timing performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Plummer and Humphrey, 2009.

claim: Movement can sharpen certain perceptual and cognitive processes.
source: On the one hand, movement can sharpen certain perceptual and cognitive processes, and on the other hand, it can introduce biasing effects on timing and on other perceptual judgments (Moher and Song, 2014), including when movement perturbations are applied (Hagura et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Moher and Song, 2014; Hagura et al., 2017.

claim: Movement can introduce biasing effects on timing and on other perceptual judgments.
source: On the one hand, movement can sharpen certain perceptual and cognitive processes, and on the other hand, it can introduce biasing effects on timing and on other perceptual judgments (Moher and Song, 2014), including when movement perturbations are applied (Hagura et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Moher and Song, 2014; Hagura et al., 2017.

claim: Motor activity can modulate sensory processing across modalities, as early as in primary sensory cortices.
source: The influence of motor activity on sensory processing is well studied–motor activity can modulate sensory processing across modalities, as early as in primary sensory cortices (for review, see Parker et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Parker et al., 2020.

claim: Locomotion can modulate gain in rodent visual and auditory cortices.
source: For example, locomotion can modulate gain in rodent visual and auditory cortices (Niell and Stryker, 2010; Zhou et al., 2014), and in humans, orientation change detection is improved when preparing to make a grasping motion aligned with the original orientation (Gutteling et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Niell and Stryker, 2010; Zhou et al., 2014.

claim: In humans, orientation change detection is improved when preparing to make a grasping motion aligned with the original orientation.
source: For example, locomotion can modulate gain in rodent visual and auditory cortices (Niell and Stryker, 2010; Zhou et al., 2014), and in humans, orientation change detection is improved when preparing to make a grasping motion aligned with the original orientation (Gutteling et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gutteling et al., 2011.

claim: Timing can be modulated by and can even be improved by movement.
source: Recent reports have shown that timing, through a neurally distributed system, is also modulated by and can even be improved by movement (Wiener et al., 2019; Carlini and French, 2014; Manning and Schutz, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wiener et al., 2019; Carlini and French, 2014; Manning and Schutz, 2013.

claim: Time is subject to distortion by externally imposed movement constraints and allowances, at least in the auditory modality and within the suprasecond range.
source: Our work confirms that time is subject to distortion by externally imposed movement constraints and allowances, at least in the auditory modality and within the suprasecond range.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Timing distortions can be modality-specific.
source: It is important to note that timing distortions can be modality-specific (Bueti, 2011), and as stated above, differ when intervals are filled versus unfilled (Iwasaki et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bueti, 2011; Iwasaki et al., 2017.
